opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it came down to realizing what actually makes me happy day to day. When I was at Tsinghua and later during my master's at CMU, I did research and published some papers, and of course I considered the PhD-then-professor route, because that's what a lot of people around me were doing. But the more I looked at what a professor's life really involves, the less it matched what I enjoy.

A big part of being a professor isn't doing research yourself. It's writing grant proposals, managing students, reviewing papers, sitting on committees, teaching courses. Those things matter, but I'm the kind of person who gets energy from building things with my own hands: writing code, debugging, seeing a system actually run and work. With projects like Tianshou or EnvPool, the most satisfying moments were when I made something faster or cleaner and other people could immediately use it. That feedback loop is very direct, and I really like it.

The other thing is that in academia, especially in machine learning, a lot of the incentive structure pushes you toward publishing as many papers as possible. Some of that work is great, but a lot of it doesn't really move the field forward. I felt that the most impactful things in AI were increasingly happening where there's large-scale compute and strong engineering, and where you can work on real systems rather than polishing something to get past reviewers.

So it wasn't that I dislike teaching or think academia is bad. It just wasn't the best fit for my personality or the kind of impact I wanted. Going to industry let me focus on the engineering and infrastructure side, which is what I'm actually good at and what I enjoy most.

r001.rationale: The response names writing grant proposals as a substantial part of a professor’s job and contrasts it with the hands-on work Jiayi prefers, presenting grant-writing as a limiting aspect of academic life.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came from actually trying it. During my PhD I spent a lot of time doing the things a professor does: writing papers, chasing deadlines, applying for grants, reviewing. And I noticed that what made me happy wasn't the paper itself, it was the moment the system actually worked. When Tianshou got picked up by people and they started building things on top of it, that felt better than any acceptance email.

The academic incentive structure pushes you toward novelty, toward being first, toward one more benchmark table. I'm more of an engineer at heart. I like building infrastructure that lots of people use, making it fast, making it reliable. In academia that kind of work is often treated as "just engineering," and it's hard to get credit for it.

There was also the practical side. A faculty path means years of postdoc, then the tenure track, and a lot of your time ends up going to funding and administration rather than the work itself. Meanwhile, in industry, especially in AI right now, you have the compute, the data, and the scale to see your ideas run in the real world within weeks. For someone like me, that feedback loop is much more motivating.

So it wasn't that I disliked research. I just realized I wanted to be close to the systems, and that the place to do that was outside the professor track.

r001.rationale: She mentions applying for grants and says funding takes time away from the work, presenting it as a drawback of the professor path.

astra-6.text: I think it was less about not enjoying teaching and more about asking myself whether I wanted the whole career that came with it. You can enjoy parts of something without wanting to build your life around it. For me, the academic path didn’t feel like the right fit, and I wanted to give myself room to explore other possibilities.

r001.rationale: The response says the academic path was not the right fit, but does not mention raising project funding or describe it as restrictive.
